opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition comes from what we've seen over and over again in deep learning: every time you introduce a hand-designed interface between two components, you're baking in an assumption about what information matters, and that assumption is almost always wrong in some way you didn't anticipate.

If you have a high-level vision-language model that outputs something like "pick up the red cup," and then a separate motor policy that executes that, the bottleneck is that language string. But so much of what matters for actually manipulating the world doesn't compress nicely into language. How heavy does the cup look? Is it slippery? Is it half-full, so it'll slosh? The planner might implicitly know a lot of that from its visual understanding, but it has no channel to pass it down. And the motor policy, conversely, can't tell the planner "hey, this grasp isn't working, I need a different approach" in any rich way.

When you train end-to-end, gradients flow through the whole system, so the model learns its own internal representations for what needs to be communicated between "deciding what to do" and "doing it." It's the same lesson as going from hand-engineered pipelines in speech recognition or translation to just training one big network. The modular systems looked more interpretable and more sensible, and they lost.

The other piece is scaling. An end-to-end model benefits from all of the pretraining, all of the world knowledge, transferring directly into control. You get positive transfer between understanding and acting. With a split architecture, you're kind of capping how much the motor side can benefit from the improvements on the cognitive side.

That said, I don't want to be dogmatic. There are practical reasons people split things today: inference latency, since you need high-frequency control and a giant model can't run at a hundred hertz, plus data scarcity on the robotics side. So you might see hierarchical systems in practice for a while. But I'd bet that, in the limit, the systems that win are ones where it's all learned jointly, even if internally they develop something that looks hierarchical. The point is that the hierarchy should be learned, not imposed.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts jointly learned end-to-end systems will win in the limit, but does not say the distinction between large and small models will disappear if large models can be trained.

r002.rationale: It mentions latency and the difficulty of running a giant model at high frequency, but does not propose using only the computation needed for a task’s complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core intuition is that every time we've drawn a hard boundary inside a system and said "this module does perception, this module does planning, this module does control," we've been imposing our own guess about where the right abstraction lies. And historically that guess has been wrong more often than it's been right. The bitter lesson keeps showing up here. The interfaces we design by hand are lossy in ways we don't anticipate.

Take the split you're describing. You have a VLM that looks at the scene and emits something like "grasp the red mug by the handle," and then a separate motor policy that's supposed to execute that. The problem is that the bottleneck between them is language, or some discrete plan representation, and that bottleneck throws away an enormous amount of information. The visual model might have a very rich sense that the mug is slightly wet, or that the handle is at an awkward angle relative to the gripper, or that there's a bit of uncertainty about where the rim actually is. None of that survives the compression into a short instruction. So the motor policy is operating partially blind, and it can't ask for clarification in any useful way. Errors compound across the interface, and neither side can learn to compensate for the other's weaknesses because the gradient doesn't flow through.

With an end-to-end model, you let the network figure out what representation is actually useful for the task. Maybe it looks something like a high-level plan internally, maybe it doesn't. The honest answer is we often find it's something we wouldn't have designed. And critically, the whole thing improves together as you scale data and compute. You're not stuck with one component being the ceiling.

Now, I want to be fair to the modular view. There are real reasons people do it. Data efficiency is the big one. You can pretrain the VLM on the entire internet and the motor policy on a comparatively small amount of robot data, and the modular design lets you get something working today. There's also interpretability and debuggability. When something goes wrong you can look at the intermediate plan and see whether perception or control failed. Those are legitimate advantages.

But I'd frame those as advantages of the current regime, not advantages in the limit. As we get more robot data, more simulation, more diverse embodiments, the data efficiency argument weakens. And I think the right way to get the benefit of internet-scale pretraining is to put it into the end-to-end model directly, rather than bolting it on as a frozen frontend. You want the same weights that understand language and images to also be the weights that produce actions, because then all of that world knowledge is available at the point where the action is chosen, with no lossy handoff.

The other thing I'd say is that the separation usually encodes an assumption that planning happens at a slow timescale and control at a fast one, and that these are cleanly different. In practice they're deeply entangled. You adjust your plan constantly based on what you feel through the gripper. A system where those loops are learned jointly can do that naturally. A system with a hard interface has to be explicitly engineered to re-plan, and you end up building a lot of scaffolding that a monolithic model would just learn.

So my bet is that modular approaches are a useful scaffold while we're data-poor, but the thing that actually works at scale is the model that sees pixels and outputs actions, with everything in between learned.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that end-to-end models improve as data and compute scale, but does not predict that the distinction between large and small models will disappear.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not propose allocating only the computation needed for a task’s complexity.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is that I don’t think we know where the right abstraction boundary is. If you have a high-level vision-language model giving instructions to a motor policy, you’ve decided in advance what information needs to pass between those systems. But a lot of manipulation depends on details that are hard to express in a high-level instruction: exactly how something is slipping, where the contact is, or whether you need to change your grip.

With an end-to-end model, the learning process can discover which details matter for the action. If it fails to pick something up, that training signal can, in principle, improve the visual representations as well as the motor behavior. You’re not relying on an interface you designed to preserve everything relevant.

That doesn’t mean everything has to run at the same frequency, or that there shouldn’t be hierarchy. You probably do want different timescales. I’d just prefer that hierarchy to emerge within something you can train jointly, rather than putting a hard boundary between reasoning and control. The modular approach can be easier to get working initially. My bet is that end-to-end has more room to improve as you scale the data and compute.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues for jointly trained end-to-end models, but does not predict that the distinction between large and small models will disappear.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions different timescales and hierarchy, but does not propose allocating computation according to task complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that I don’t think we know the right abstraction boundary. If you have a high-level model that looks at the scene and tells a motor policy what to do, you’ve made a pretty strong assumption about what information needs to pass between those two systems. And a lot of what matters for control is quite subtle—whether something is slipping, how contact is changing, whether you need to adjust your grip. You want the model’s understanding of the task to be informed by those details, and you want the motor behavior to benefit from that understanding.

With end-to-end training, the system can learn what information it needs to represent, and errors in the eventual action can improve the representations upstream. You’re not relying on us to hand-design the interface correctly.

That doesn’t mean the model has to do all its reasoning at the same frequency as its motor control. You can have different timescales and internal structure. I’m more skeptical of making those components separate learning problems with a fixed interface between them. That can be a very useful engineering shortcut, but I’d expect jointly trained systems to have a higher ceiling.

r001.rationale: The response discusses end-to-end training and fixed interfaces, but does not predict that the distinction between large and small models will disappear.

r002.rationale: The response mentions different reasoning and motor-control timescales, but does not propose allocating computation according to task complexity.
